title: Senior's toolkit: inspecting TLS
summary: See which certificate and chain a server really sends, which names and dates it has, which versions and ALPN it speaks, and how to test without turning checks off.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: inspecting TLS
steps.body: Most TLS errors are one of four things: the wrong name, an expired certificate, a missing intermediate, or a version or cipher mismatch. These commands show each one directly.

toolkit.what: Does a real TLS handshake and prints the chain the server sent, the negotiated version and cipher, and `Verify return code`.
flags: send SNI; OpenSSL 1.1.1+ sets it from a host name in `-connect`, but never for an IP, and then many servers return a default certificate
print every certificate the server sent, not just the leaf
close the connection right after the handshake
fail the handshake if verification fails

toolkit.what: Reads the leaf certificate's names and validity straight from the live server.
flags: the DNS names it is valid for (the CN is ignored by clients)
exit 1 if it expires within 10 days
toolkit.example: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

toolkit.what: Forces one protocol version. Proves whether an old client fails because the server dropped TLS 1.2, or a scanner flags TLS 1.0 still being on.
flags: offer ALPN protocols; the output shows `ALPN protocol: h2`
one-paragraph summary of what was negotiated

toolkit.what: Trusts a specific CA for one call: the right way to test a service with a private CA. `-k` turns all checks off and hides the real problem.
flags: no verification: only for a quick look, never in scripts

toolkit.what: Lists every TLS version and cipher suite the server accepts, with a grade. A quick audit before a security review (scan only hosts you are allowed to).
Inspects TLS on protocols that upgrade a plain connection: SMTP, IMAP, PostgreSQL and others.

steps.prompt: Match each symptom to the command that confirms it.
pairs: An old client fails, new ones work

steps.prompt: Browsers open `https://api.example.com` fine, but the .NET service and `curl` fail with `unable to get local issuer certificate`. `openssl s_client -showcerts` shows only one certificate. What is wrong?
options: The server sends only the leaf, not the intermediate. Browsers often fill the gap from cache; other clients cannot. Serve the full chain (fullchain.pem)
steps.explain: A server must send its leaf plus the intermediates. Browsers cache intermediates and can fetch them, which hides the mistake; most libraries do not.

steps.prompt: `openssl s_client -connect 10.0.4.21:443` shows a certificate for `default.example.net`, but the site is `shop.example.com`. Browsers see the right certificate. What did you forget?
options: `-servername shop.example.com`, so the server knows which site you want (SNI)
steps.explain: One IP often hosts many sites. Without SNI the server picks a default certificate. Browsers always send SNI; openssl only does when it knows the name.

steps.prompt: Print the names and expiry date of the certificate `api.example.com` actually serves.
steps.code: openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -__1__ api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl __2__ -noout -__3__ -ext subjectAltName
steps.explain: `-servername` sends SNI, `x509` parses the PEM coming down the pipe, and `-enddate` prints `notAfter`. `-dates` would also work.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When a TLS error appears, run `openssl s_client -servername ... -showcerts` before you change anything: the name, dates and chain are right there. Never "fix" it with `-k` or a disabled check in code; use `--cacert` for private CAs and fix the server's chain.
